title: Compare the major architecture styles — Monolith, Modular Monolith, Microservices, Layered (N-Tier), Microkernel/Plugin, Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters), Space-Based, Peer-to-Peer — and the problem each one actually solves.
shortTitle: Compare the major architecture styles — Monolith, Modular Monolith, Microservices, Layered, Microkernel, Hexagonal, Space-Based, Peer-to-Peer — and the problem each one solves.

s1_definition.profdef: An architecture style is a high-level pattern for how a system is structured, deployed, and how its parts communicate. The major styles each solve a different primary problem. A Monolith is one deployable unit and solves simplicity. A Modular Monolith keeps one deployable but enforces internal module boundaries, solving maintainability without distribution. Microservices split into independently deployable services, solving independent scaling and team autonomy at the cost of distributed complexity. Layered (N-Tier) organizes code into horizontal layers, solving separation of concerns. Microkernel/Plugin has a stable core plus plugins, solving extensibility. Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters) isolates domain logic from infrastructure, solving testability and technology independence. Space-Based uses an in-memory data grid, solving extreme load by removing the database bottleneck. Peer-to-Peer has no central coordinator, solving decentralization.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India as a building. A Monolith is one big open-plan office where everyone works in one room — simple but crowded. A Modular Monolith is the same building but with clearly walled departments so teams do not step on each other. Microservices are separate buildings across the city, each department independent. Layered is one building with floors — reception on the ground, officers above, the vault at the bottom. Microkernel is a bank core with pluggable product modules you can add or remove (loans, insurance). Hexagonal is a department designed so it does not care whether customers arrive by phone, web, or in person, and does not care whether records are in Oracle or a file — the business rules sit in the middle, untouched. Space-Based is a trading floor that keeps everything in fast memory because the vault is too slow for the rush. Peer-to-Peer is a network of branches that gossip directly with no head office.
s1_definition.oneliner: Every architecture style exists to solve one dominant problem — pick the style whose problem matches yours, because choosing the wrong one buys complexity you do not need.

**Professional definition:** An architecture style is a high-level pattern for how a system is structured, deployed, and how its parts communicate. The major styles each solve a different primary problem. A Monolith is one deployable unit and solves simplicity. A Modular Monolith keeps one deployable but enforces internal module boundaries, solving maintainability without distribution. Layered (N-Tier) organizes code into horizontal layers, solving separation of concerns. Microkernel/Plugin has a stable core plus plugins, solving extensibility. Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters) isolates domain logic from infrastructure, solving testability and technology independence. Space-Based uses an in-memory data grid, solving extreme load by removing the database bottleneck. Peer-to-Peer has no central coordinator, solving decentralization.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India as a building. A Monolith is one big open-plan office where everyone works in one room — simple but crowded. A Modular Monolith is the same building but with clearly walled departments so teams do not step on each other. Microservices are separate buildings across the city, each department independent. Layered is one building with floors — reception on the ground, officers above, the vault at the bottom. Microkernel is a bank core with pluggable product modules you can add or remove (loans, insurance). Hexagonal is a department designed so it does not care whether customers arrive by phone, web, or in person, and does not care whether records are in Oracle or a file — the business rules sit in the middle, untouched. Space-Based is a trading floor that keeps everything in fast memory because the vault is too slow for the rush. Peer-to-Peer is a network of branches that gossip directly with no head office.

**One line to remember:** Every architecture style exists to solve one dominant problem — pick the style whose problem matches yours, because choosing the wrong one buys complexity you do not need.

sections.s2_technical:
A Monolith packages the entire application — all features, all layers — into one deployable artifact running in one process. The problem it solves is simplicity: one codebase, one build, one deploy, in-process calls with no network, and easy transactions. It is the right default for small teams and early products. Its weakness is that as it grows, everything is coupled, one bug can take down everything, and you must scale the whole thing even if only one feature is hot.

A Modular Monolith is still one deployable, but internally it is split into well-defined modules with enforced boundaries, each module exposing a clear interface and hiding its internals. The problem it solves is maintainability and future-proofing: you get clean separation and the option to later extract a module into a microservice, while keeping the operational simplicity of a single deployment. It is the recommended starting point for most systems before jumping to microservices.

Microservices split the system into many small, independently deployable services, each owning its own data and communicating over the network via REST, gRPC, or messaging. The problem they solve is independent deployment, independent scaling, team autonomy, and polyglot technology. The cost is distributed systems complexity: network failures, eventual consistency, distributed tracing, and heavy operational overhead. They pay off only when you have multiple teams that genuinely need to deploy and scale independently.

Layered (N-Tier) is an organizing principle more than a deployment style: code is arranged in horizontal layers — presentation, business, persistence, database — where each layer only talks to the one below. The problem it solves is separation of concerns and testability of each layer. It can be applied inside a monolith or inside each microservice.

Microkernel (Plugin) architecture has a minimal stable core plus plugins that add features. The problem it solves is extensibility: you add capabilities without touching the core. IDEs, browsers, content management systems, and rules engines use this. In banking, a core transaction engine with pluggable product modules (loans, cards, insurance) fits.

Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters) puts the domain logic in the center, defines ports (interfaces) for everything it needs, and attaches adapters on the outside for specific technologies (REST adapter, Kafka adapter, JPA adapter). The problem it solves is isolating business logic from infrastructure so you can swap technologies and test the domain in isolation. It is a style you layer inside a service, not an alternative to microservices.

Space-Based architecture keeps application state in an in-memory data grid replicated across nodes rather than hammering a central database, which is the usual bottleneck under extreme load. The problem it solves is extreme, bursty, high-volume load — trading systems, ticket sales, flash sales. Writes go to memory and are asynchronously flushed to the database. It is justified only when the database genuinely cannot keep up.

Peer-to-Peer architecture has no central coordinator; every node is both client and server and nodes talk directly. The problem it solves is decentralization as a hard requirement — blockchain, file sharing, mesh networks. It trades away the simplicity of a central authority for resilience and censorship-resistance.

A senior nuance is that these styles are not mutually exclusive. A real banking system is often microservices (deployment style), where each service is internally layered or hexagonal (code organization style), one service might be a microkernel (the product engine), and a hot trading service might be space-based. Choosing a style is choosing which problem to prioritize, and the classic mistake is adopting microservices for their resume value when a modular monolith would have served better.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is growing and the architecture team must decide how to structure new systems. They need a simple model that captures each style and the problem it solves so they can reason about trade-offs.

Problem 1 — The accidental microservice. A team split a tiny new feature into six microservices because it was fashionable. They then spent months fighting distributed tracing and eventual consistency for a feature two people could have built as a module. This is the classic mismatch — using microservices (which solve independent scaling and team autonomy) for a problem that only needed simplicity. A modular monolith was the right fit.

Problem 2 — The frozen trading desk. The trading system used a central database, and during market-open bursts the database became the bottleneck and orders queued. This is exactly the problem space-based architecture solves: extreme bursty load where the database cannot keep up, fixed by an in-memory data grid.

We will model the styles as a small decision engine. Each architecture style is represented as an object that knows the problem it solves, its main cost, and whether it fits a given scenario. A `StyleAdvisor` takes a scenario (team size, load profile, decentralization need) and recommends a style with reasoning.

The code will have an `ArchitectureStyle` abstraction, concrete styles (Monolith, ModularMonolith, Microservices, SpaceBased, PeerToPeer, and so on), a `Scenario` describing requirements, and a `StyleAdvisor` that picks and explains. The demo runs the two banking scenarios above and prints the recommended style and why.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three scenarios — a small savings-goal feature (2 engineers, low load), a market-open order burst (30 engineers, extreme load), and inter-bank settlement (10 engineers, needs decentralization).

Step 1 — The advisor evaluates scenarios in priority order, checking the hardest constraints first: decentralization, then extreme load, then team autonomy.

Step 2 — The small feature has low load, a tiny team, no decentralization. It does not fit Peer-to-Peer, Space-Based, or Microservices, but fits Modular Monolith. The advisor recommends Modular Monolith and explains it solves maintainability with single-deploy simplicity.

Step 3 — The trading burst has extreme load. The first style whose fit returns true is Space-Based, because its whole purpose is removing the database bottleneck under extreme load. The advisor recommends Space-Based.

Step 4 — The settlement scenario needs decentralization, so Peer-to-Peer fits first. The advisor recommends Peer-to-Peer and names its cost: harder consistency and no central authority.

Step 5 — Each recommendation carries the problem it solves and its main cost, so the architect sees the trade-off, not just a label.

```
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] Scenario 'New savings-goal feature' (team=2, load=low, decentralized=false) → Modular Monolith
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO]    Solves: Maintainability + clean boundaries with single-deploy simplicity
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO]    Cost:   One deploy; discipline needed to keep module boundaries
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I think of architecture styles as each solving one dominant problem, and the skill is matching the style to the problem rather than following fashion. A monolith solves pure simplicity — one build, one deploy, in-process calls — and is the right default for a small team. A modular monolith keeps that single-deployment simplicity but enforces internal module boundaries, solving maintainability, and it is the starting point I recommend for most systems because you can extract a module into a service later if you truly need to. Microservices solve independent deployment, independent scaling, team autonomy, and polyglot technology, but they cost you distributed complexity, eventual consistency, and heavy operational overhead, so they only pay off with multiple teams that genuinely need that independence.

The layered style is about organizing code into horizontal tiers for separation of concerns, and it lives inside a monolith or inside each microservice rather than being a deployment choice. The microkernel style is a stable core plus plugins, solving extensibility, which fits a banking product engine where loans, cards, and insurance are plugins added without touching the core. The hexagonal style puts the domain in the center with ports and adapters around it, solving isolation of business logic from infrastructure so I can swap technologies and test the domain alone, and it is something I layer inside a service, not an alternative to microservices.

Space-based architecture keeps state in an in-memory data grid to remove the database bottleneck, and it is justified only under extreme bursty load like trading or ticketing where the database genuinely cannot keep up. Peer-to-peer has no central coordinator and solves decentralization as a hard requirement, as in blockchain or file sharing, trading the simplicity of a central authority for resilience.

The senior point I always make is that these styles are not mutually exclusive. A real bank platform is often microservices at the deployment level, with each service organized internally as layered or hexagonal, one service built as a microkernel product engine, a hot trading path built space-based, and an inter-bank settlement network built peer-to-peer. The classic mistake is reaching for microservices because they look impressive when a modular monolith would have solved the actual problem with far less pain.

The one-line summary I give is that every architecture style exists to solve one specific problem, so you pick the style whose problem matches yours, you combine styles across deployment and code-organization dimensions, and you avoid buying distributed complexity you do not need.
